posts.title: 12 Factors Texas Judges Consider in Child Custody Cases
posts.metaTitle: 12 Factors Texas Judges Consider in Custody Cases
posts.metaDescription: Facing a custody hearing in Texas? Learn the 12 factors judges weigh, the difference between conservatorship and possession, and how to prepare. Free confidential consultation.
keywords: best interest of the child Texas
posts.imageAlt: Parent holding a young child's hand — Texas child custody factors
intro: If you're heading into a custody case in Texas, one of the most common questions parents ask is: what is the judge actually looking at? Texas courts don't use a rigid formula — instead, judges weigh a range of factors to determine what arrangement serves the "best interest of the child," a legal standard that gives courts broad discretion.

Knowing what the court is looking for before you walk into that hearing can change how you prepare, what evidence you gather, and how you present your case. Below are the 12 factors Texas judges may consider, plus a breakdown of two terms that are often confused but mean very different things: conservatorship and possession.

blocks.text: The court's first priority is always the child — not either parent's preferences or convenience.

**1. Emotional and physical needs of the child.** Judges look at the child's day-to-day needs, including health, developmental stage, schooling, and emotional stability, and which parent is better positioned to meet them.
**2. The child's relationship with each parent.** Courts consider the existing bond between the child and each parent, including who has historically handled caretaking responsibilities.
**3. The child's relationship with siblings.** Keeping siblings together is often a priority, and judges will factor in the impact a custody arrangement would have on sibling relationships.

**4. The child's own preferences, if age-appropriate.** In Texas, a child who is 12 or older can request to speak with the judge about their custody preference. While not the deciding factor, the court can take the child's wishes into account.
Beyond the child, courts also evaluate each parent's capacity to provide a safe, stable, and nurturing environment.
**5. Stability of each parent's home environment.** This includes housing stability, routine, and whether the environment supports the child's wellbeing.
**6. Parenting skills and ability to nurture.** Judges consider each parent's demonstrated ability to care for the child's physical, emotional, and educational needs.
**7. Work schedule and availability.** A parent's job demands and flexibility to be present for the child factor into the court's assessment.
**8. Geographic proximity of each parent.** Distance between parents' homes can affect school logistics, visitation schedules, and the practicality of shared custody.
Safety concerns and each parent's willingness to support the child's relationship with the other parent carry significant weight.
**9. History of domestic violence or abuse.** Any documented history of violence or abuse is a serious factor and can significantly limit or restrict a parent's custody or visitation rights.
**10. History of substance abuse.** Courts assess whether substance abuse issues, past or present, could affect a parent's ability to safely care for the child.

**11. Any false allegations made by either parent.** Texas courts take false allegations seriously — making unfounded claims to gain an advantage in a custody case can damage a parent's credibility and case.

**12. Willingness to support the child's relationship with the other parent.** Texas courts generally favor arrangements that allow the child to maintain a relationship with both parents. A parent who actively undermines that relationship can be viewed unfavorably by the court.

sections.heading: Know the Difference: Conservatorship vs. Possession

blocks.text: These two terms are often used interchangeably by parents going through a custody case — but they mean very different things, and it's important to understand both.

**Conservatorship = who makes decisions.** This covers legal decision-making authority over things like the child's education, healthcare, and religious upbringing. Parents can be named joint managing conservators (sharing decision-making) or one parent may be named sole managing conservator.

**Possession = where the child lives and the visitation schedule.** This determines the physical custody arrangement — where the child primarily resides and the schedule for time with the other parent.

**The key thing to understand: you can share one without the other.** It's entirely possible for parents to share joint decision-making authority (conservatorship) while one parent has primary physical custody (possession), or for the visitation schedule to look very different from the decision-making split. Confusing the two — or assuming a 50/50 decision-making role guarantees 50/50 time with the child — is one of the most common misunderstandings parents bring into a custody case.

sections.heading: Your Relationship With Your Child Is Worth Fighting For

blocks.text: Custody cases are emotional, high-stakes, and often confusing to navigate alone. Understanding these 12 factors is a starting point — but every case is different, and how you present your circumstances matters.

faqs.q: What factors do Texas judges consider in child custody cases?
faqs.a: Texas judges weigh 12 key factors across three categories: the child's needs and relationships (emotional/physical needs, relationships with parents and siblings, and the child's own preference if age-appropriate), each parent's situation (home stability, parenting skills, work schedule, and geographic proximity), and safety and co-parenting ability (history of abuse, substance abuse, false allegations, and willingness to support the other parent's relationship with the child).

faqs.q: What is the "best interest of the child" standard in Texas?
faqs.a: This is the legal standard Texas courts use to make custody decisions. Rather than a fixed formula, judges consider a range of factors — including the 12 listed above — to determine which arrangement best supports the child's wellbeing.

faqs.q: Can a child choose which parent to live with in Texas?
faqs.a: A child who is 12 or older can request to speak with the judge about their custody preference. However, this is only one factor among many and is not the deciding factor in the court's decision.

faqs.q: What's the difference between conservatorship and possession in Texas?
faqs.a: Conservatorship refers to legal decision-making authority over things like education, healthcare, and religion. Possession refers to where the child physically lives and the visitation schedule. Parents can share one without sharing the other.

faqs.q: Does a history of domestic violence affect custody in Texas?
faqs.a: Yes. A documented history of domestic violence or abuse is a significant factor that can limit or restrict a parent's custody or visitation rights.

faqs.q: What happens if a parent makes false allegations during a custody case?
faqs.a: Texas courts take false allegations seriously. Making unfounded claims against the other parent to gain an advantage can damage the accusing parent's credibility and negatively affect their case.

posts.metaTitle: Getting Divorced in Texas? How Property & Debt Get Divided
posts.metaDescription: Texas is a community property state — here's what that means for your assets, debts, and what might be protected in a divorce. Free consultation with a family law attorney.
posts.imageAlt: Couple reviewing and signing a divorce settlement agreement — Texas property and debt division
intro: Divorce is stressful enough without wondering what happens to your house, your savings, or the debt on your joint credit card. In Texas, the rules around who gets what are different from many other states — and understanding them before you agree to anything can make a significant difference in your outcome.

sections.heading: Texas Is a Community Property State

blocks.text: Texas follows **community property law**, which means most assets and debts acquired during the marriage are considered to belong equally to both spouses — regardless of whose name is on the account, the title, or the loan.

This surprises a lot of people. Even if you opened a credit card in your own name, or a bank account only you deposit into, it can still be classified as community property if it was acquired during the marriage.

sections.heading: What Gets Divided? More Than You Might Think

blocks.text: Community property division typically covers:
Retirement accounts and business interests are often the most overlooked — and the most contested — because their value isn't always obvious without a proper valuation.

That said, separate property can lose its protected status if it becomes "commingled" with community property — for example, depositing inheritance funds into a joint account. Keeping clear records matters.

sections.heading: Know What You're Entitled to Before You Agree to Anything

blocks.text: Property division in a Texas divorce isn't always a simple 50/50 split, and it's easy to accept less than you're entitled to — or take on more debt than you should — without realizing it. Before signing any agreement, it's worth understanding exactly what's on the table.

faqs.q: Is Texas a community property state?
faqs.a: Yes. In Texas, most assets and debts acquired during the marriage are considered community property, owned equally by both spouses, regardless of whose name is on the account or title.

faqs.q: What property is divided in a Texas divorce?
faqs.a: Community property division can include income earned during the marriage, the family home, retirement accounts and 401(k)s, business interests and investments, and credit card or loan debt.

faqs.q: What property is protected from division in a Texas divorce?
faqs.a: Separate property is generally protected, including property owned before the marriage, gifts received during the marriage, inheritances left to one spouse, and anything covered by a valid prenuptial agreement.

faqs.q: Can separate property become community property in Texas?
faqs.a: Yes. Separate property can lose its protected status if it becomes commingled with community property — for example, mixing inheritance funds into a joint bank account.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to divide property in a Texas divorce?
faqs.a: While not legally required, a family law attorney can help ensure you understand what you're entitled to and don't unknowingly accept an unfair settlement. Hirani Law Firm offers a free consultation to review your situation.

posts.metaTitle: Injured in a Car Accident in Texas? 4 Steps to Protect Your Case
posts.metaDescription: Been in a car accident in Texas? Learn the 4 critical steps to take in the first 72 hours to protect your health and your legal claim. Free consultation, no fees unless we win.
keywords: what to do after a car accident in Texas
posts.imageAlt: Two-car collision with an overturned SUV — what to do after a car accident in Texas
intro: Car accidents happen fast — but what you do in the hours and days afterward can determine whether you receive full compensation or nothing at all. Insurance companies look for any excuse to reduce or deny a claim, and small mistakes made in the immediate aftermath of a crash are often the reason valid claims get denied.
If you've been injured in a car accident in Texas, here are the four steps that matter most.

blocks.text: Even if the accident seems minor, call 911 and get a police report filed at the scene.

**Why it matters:** No official report means no official record — and insurance companies can and will use the absence of a police report against you when disputing a claim. A police report creates a neutral, timestamped account of what happened, which becomes critical evidence later.

sections.heading: Step 2: See a Doctor Within 24–48 Hours

blocks.text: Adrenaline masks pain. It's common to feel "fine" right after a crash and then develop symptoms of whiplash or internal injuries days later.

**Why it matters:** Delaying medical care doesn't just put your health at risk — it gives insurance companies a reason to argue your injuries weren't caused by the accident, or weren't serious to begin with. A prompt medical record links your injury directly to the crash.
Once you and everyone involved are safe, take these actions to preserve your ability to recover full compensation:

list: Take photos of the scene, vehicles, injuries, and road conditions
Collect witness names and contact information
Save all medical records and documents
**Do NOT** give a recorded statement to the insurance company
**Do NOT** accept any settlement offer without an attorney

blocks.text: Insurance adjusters are trained to get recorded statements and early settlement offers that minimize what they have to pay. Once you accept an offer, you typically can't go back for more — even if your injuries turn out to be worse than expected.

faqs.q: What should I do immediately after a car accident in Texas?
faqs.a: Call 911 to report the accident and ensure a police report is filed, even if the accident seems minor. This creates an official record that protects you if the insurance company later disputes your claim.

faqs.q: How soon after a car accident should I see a doctor?
faqs.a: Within 24–48 hours. Adrenaline can mask pain and injuries like whiplash or internal trauma often don't show symptoms right away. Prompt medical treatment also links your injuries directly to the accident in your medical record.

faqs.q: Should I give a recorded statement to the insurance company?
faqs.a: No. Insurance companies use recorded statements to find ways to reduce or deny your claim. Speak with a personal injury attorney before providing any statement.

faqs.q: Should I accept a settlement offer from the insurance company?
faqs.a: Not without consulting an attorney first. Early settlement offers are often far lower than what you're actually entitled to, and once accepted, you typically cannot seek additional compensation later.
